bd37e3ae7411cbea: MANCHESTER: Former Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola threw his weight behind the club on Wednesday after a bombshell verdict on Premier League financial rule breaches plunged their future into serious doubt.

The former boss broke his silence 24 hours after it was announced that the Abu Dhabi-backed club had been found guilty of more than 100 breaches of financial rules in the world's richest domestic league.
Premier League chief executive Richard Masters described the disciplinary case and the decision by an independent commission as the "most significant in Premier League history."
He said City "systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade", adding that the league was committed to a swift resolution.
The likely punishment is uncertain but, according to Premier League rules, City could face a substantial points deduction, a fine or even expulsion from the top division.
The 10-time English champions, who continue to deny any wrongdoing, have vowed to appeal and have until Friday to do so.
Guardiola, who was a vocal supporter of the club over the issue before leaving the Etihad in May, broke his silence in a post on X.
"I want every single @ManCity fan to know I am here, more than ever," said the Spaniard, who won six Premier League titles and the Champions League in a golden decade at the helm.
"I am, always have been, always will be, behind my club, my owner, my chairman, (CEO) Ferran (Soriano), the players, staff, (manager) Enzo (Maresca) and you, our unique supporters.
"Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all."
The Premier League, which first charged City in 2023, announced the findings of the commission on Tuesday.

The commission found City arranged "sham" deals to artificially inflate revenues and reduce costs by more than £900 million ($1.2 billion) between 2009 and 2018, a period in which they won three Premier League titles and other silverware.
In doing so they concealed the true state of their finances but the commission said the club were "significantly in breach of both the Premier League's and UEFA's spending limits."
The commission found the club guilty on all charges related to breaches of financial rules over the nine-year period.
They have also been found guilty of most of the charges they faced in relation to a failure to cooperate with a Premier League investigation.
Punishment
Everton and Nottingham Forest were given points deductions in the 2023/24 season for single breaches of financial sustainability rules.
On that basis, City could face relegation given the sheer weight of the case against them.
There is speculation they could even be stripped of their titles.
"If the appeal fails, Manchester City cannot stay in the league, they have to suffer. And I say that as a supporter and a fan," said the club's former chairman, David Bernstein.
Another factor is a potential flood of compensation claims. Former Liverpool managing director Christian Purslow told the BBC that clubs would be "queueing up to seek compensation."
Former City defender Micah Richards, who was part of the side that won the club's first top-flight league title for 44 years in 2012, said the uncertainty was "heartbreaking."
"The reports were troubling. I saw the words which were used by the Premier League in sham contracts and I felt absolutely devastated," Richards said on The Rest is Football podcast.

"I've been at that club since I was 14 years old, I would die for that club. I achieved my dream at Manchester City, but then to hear these reports, and not only me as an ex-player, but the fans, what they have to go through, absolutely devastating."
City have become the Premier League's dominant force since the 2008 takeover by Sheikh Mansour, the vice-president and deputy prime minister of the United Arab Emirates.
The team are next in action against Liverpool at Anfield on October 11, where they will take on the club who have been their closest challengers over the past decade.

dd892fd4397cb132: THE exciting return of Formula 1 to Sepang this weekend, as an understudy for Bahrain during the Middle East conflict, reignites a debate thought settled nine years ago.

In the mid-1990s, Malaysia was establishing itself as Southeast Asia's rising economy, determined to put itself on the map. F1 has always been a one-stop shop for global brand awareness: Petronas began backing a team in 1995, and Visit Malaysia appeared on another from 1997.

Winning a slot on the calendar of the world's largest annual global sport was a different order of magnitude. As with attracting multinational corporations to a country, it demands long-term commitment and infrastructure investment. Building a circuit for F1 alongside the capital's airport was a strong move. In October 1999, Malaysia arrived on the world championship stage. Drivers rated Sepang, fans loved it - and Kuala Lumpur became a popular stop.
How different it seemed by 2017. Judged against a backdrop of rising race-hosting fees, the Grand Prix looked less compelling.

The first mover advantage, and much of the benefit, had already been banked. Sepang, originally one of only 16 races, was now one of 20 - with even more slated to join the calendar. Worse, Malaysia was no longer unique in Southeast Asia. And, of all its neighbours, the newcomer was its sibling rival, Singapore - just down the road. Making the comparison as unflattering as possible, it previewed F1's future: the Grand Prix as a festival. Racing at night took the sting out of equatorial heat and turned the city into a floodlit postcard. Scheduling Sepang immediately after Marina Bay, in 2016 and 2017, must have been the final straw.
Stepping off the calendar is easy to understand. Ending a brand campaign after 19 consecutive years, its original ambition achieved, meets any reasonable measure of marketing consistency.
Of course, few foresaw what followed. Liberty Media bought the championship in 2017 and set about turning every race into a Super Bowl.

Initiatives such as Netflix's Drive to Survive drew new audiences. With everyone at home during the pandemic, viewers binged the series and, when F1 became the first global sport back on the road, they tuned in to the live racing too.
The fan base has grown by more than 60 per cent since the takeover, to 827 million. Women now make up 42 per cent, up from under a third in 2019, and the audience is markedly younger.

What Malaysia bought into in 1999 now provides even greater returns. A Grand Prix still associates a country with a premier sporting endeavour where technology meets entertainment. The difference is a larger, more valuable audience. Judging those returns by gate receipts misses the point: the real value lies in years of recognition that draws tourists and investors. Today, calling a race overpriced says more about a host's ability to extract value than about the cost.
Some will argue that, with the prize greater than ever and the venue proven and ready, Malaysia should bring F1 back permanently.

The practical answer is that, even with the calendar now stretched to 24 races, supply falls well short of demand. Existing races are signing longer renewals to secure their position. Few are leaving, and more want in. In Asia alone, Thailand, Korea and India have each held talks with F1 recently. Osaka has proposed taking the Japanese round from Suzuka. Whilst none is imminent, it is clear why hosting fees continue to rise.
Even if there were a slot, and Malaysia accepted today's asking price, F1 would likely lean towards markets with strategic advantages - such as unlocking a new fan base.

The good news is that Malaysia already has a place on a world championship calendar: MotoGP's. And last year Liberty Media, the company that transformed F1, completed its purchase of the motorcycle championship.

Last time, Malaysia left just as Liberty arrived. This time it is already on the grid. So too are Thailand and Indonesia, but Buriram and Mandalika are far from their capitals, whilst Sepang sits at the gateway to KL. That is a head start worth building on.
The writer is a Singapore-based motorsport expert. A former racing driver and familiar face to Formula 1 television viewers across Asia, he now advises brands on motorsport partnerships

748de2112c17524e: According to the US President, the term Artificial Intelligence (AI) is tired while "Super Intelligence" is wired. Trump has issued an executive order to compel the Federal Government to use the new name instead. The term Artificial Intelligence was introduced by American computer and cognitive scientist John McCarthy in 1956, although the concept derives at least in part from work by British mathematician Alan Turing published in 1950. Regardless of its origin, the technology has outgrown the term, and the US, in particular, should adopt a new one, according to the man in the Oval Office. “The capabilities of today’s frontier systems do much more than imitate or automate discrete aspects of human intelligence. They increasingly amplify human ingenuity and unlock new forms of creativity, empowering Americans to achieve what was previously impossible across science, medicine, and nearly every other domain of human endeavor," he said in an executive order, which has the power to direct Federal agencies' behavior. "As these capabilities continue to improve, they increasingly represent not merely artificial intelligence, but a new era of Super Intelligence,” he added. Accordingly, the order directs federal government to “reflect the transformative capabilities of these technologies and the limitless opportunities they create for the American people”. Trump said that because “Super Intelligence” is more apt for “advancing capabilities of these technologies”, the executive branch should use the terms “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in place of “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI”. The order says the executive branch “will not acknowledge the usage of 'Artificial Intelligence' and 'AI' in any applicable setting”. The president also orders that government websites, official correspondence, public communications and policy documents reflect this change. The question is why the sudden change? It was only in June that Trump issued an executive order to promote “artificial intelligence innovation and security”. It orders the “upgrading of American systems for advanced AI” and promises Federal Government access to “frontier models”. We’re guessing all that paperwork will now have to be pulped. Others are speculating about motives aside from any sudden leap forward in technology over the last three months or so. Posting on X, Adam Cochran, a managing partner at Canadian VC firm Cinneamhain Ventures, claimed the decision to publish the executive order could be linked to investments in the .si domains over the last three months, which he argued would rise in popularity among governments and companies wishing to curry favor with the US administration. Although unable to produce categorical evidence that these investments could be linked to the President, his family or business associates, Cochran pointed toward a spike in domain registrations with the suffix .si, including 12,000 MAGA-related domains. In the few months leading up to the announcement, people also registered more than 10,000 AI-related terms to the .si domains, he claimed, some of which, he added, have now been relisted for millions of dollars. In the absence of any overriding evidence, a right-thinking person is forced to weigh the most likely explanation, balancing the probability that the US has entered the era of super intelligence and must change its paperwork and website registration accordingly to maintain its technological superiority, against the chance that the executive order is part of a shameless domain-name grift. ®

ebc186440ce24fa4: INDIA'S drive to verify the eligibility of roughly a billion voters has put the Election Commission of India (ECI) under severe public scrutiny, with opposition parties alleging the manipulation of voter rolls and exclusion of millions.

A report published last week by the Indian Express newspaper alleged there were internal divisions within the election body over the lists and registration procedures, stoking further concerns about its neutrality.
Last Friday saw nationwide protests by the opposition Congress party demanding the resignation of the head of the ECI, Gyanesh Kumar.
The "cockroach" youth movement, with millions of supporters, has also said it would launch protests across India tomorrow if Kumar ​does not resign.
India started verification of its voter rolls last year ahead of elections in the eastern state of Bihar. The review has now covered the majority of Indian states.

While voter roll revisions are routine, this round became controversial after large numbers of voters in states such as Bihar and West Bengal found their names missing from electoral rolls and were unable to cast ballots.
Opposition parties, including Congress, have accused Kumar of bias and alleged that the process benefits Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The election body and the BJP denied such claims.
The Indian Express story said two top election commissioners had expressed concerns to Kumar at least 14 times in 10 months but those concerns were not taken into consideration.
The ECI said all its decisions were lawful and differing views within the commission were not unusual.

The report has prompted some opposition leaders and members of the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), which in July forced the education minister to quit after weeks of protest, to plan nationwide demonstrations in the coming days demanding Kumar's resignation.

Local media has reported that the verification drive has resulted in around 130 million people being excluded from the first draft list, and are being required to prove their credentials before being enrolled.
ECI data showed that about 6.5 million voters were excluded from the draft rolls during Bihar's revision exercise last year.
India's Supreme Court has also raised concerns, saying notices to prove eligibility sent to some voters appeared to have been "machine generated" without human intervention, local media reported.
The ECI says names are only removed when a voter has died, is mentioned more than once on the rolls, has moved to another region, or is untraceable.
Officers are required to record detailed reasons why a voter is deleted.
People whose names do not appear in draft rolls can request inclusion before final voter lists are published and also raise appeals if such requests are denied.
Voters excluded from final rolls can also challenge the decision.
To participate in future elections, excluded voters must succeed in their appeals or apply for fresh registration.
Opposition parties argue that arbitrary deletions and lengthy appeals prevented millions in Bihar and West Bengal from voting and could be used as a weapon in future elections.
At least seven Indian states will hold elections next year, including Uttar Pradesh, considered a bellwether state in national politics.
Verification in Uttar Pradesh began last October and saw 13 per cent of names being deleted, according to local media reports.
The ECI has defended itself from allegations of political bias, including in a rare press conference by Kumar last year who asked the opposition to submit their allegations under oath.

On Saturday, the election body announced revisions to the process, including home visits by officials to collect verification documents and an extension of the deadline for final verification in some states.
The writer is from Reuters

15bfa76220916af0: THE world's biggest energy companies are poised to deliver another quarter of bumper profits, fuelled by record refining margins.
Flush with cash, Big Oil now needs to chart a course for future growth in a world reshaped by the Middle East crisis.

The five largest Western oil companies — BP, Chevron, Exxon Mobil, Shell and TotalEnergies — are expected to report combined third-quarter profits of around US$53 billion, according to RBC Capital Markets estimates, up from US$48 billion in the second quarter and more than double year-earlier levels.
Yet since the start of the Iran war in late February, oil majors have largely reacted cautiously to this windfall, directing billions towards debt reduction rather than major new investments.

What began as a confrontation between the United States, Israel and Iran has evolved into a protracted, low-intensity regional conflict characterised by attacks on energy infrastructure, refineries and shipping lanes.

Many of the consequences for global energy markets — including a higher geopolitical risk premium, altered supply lines and greater energy nationalism — are likely to linger long after the fighting ends.
That changes the calculus for an industry that makes multibillion-dollar investment decisions with time horizons measured in decades.
Among the majors, Exxon stands to benefit the most given its refining capacity of roughly four million barrels per day, the largest among the majors.
The refining boom represents a remarkable reversal for a segment of the industry that many executives had viewed as a low-priority business.
Over the past decade, majors reduced their refining exposure amid concerns about emissions, weak returns and uncertain long-term fuel demand.
Will the Middle East crisis change this? Not entirely.

Companies remain unlikely to build new refineries in Europe or North America, given the challenging economics. But investing in new capacity in Asia or Africa has become significantly more attractive, particularly when linked to long-term supply and purchase agreements.
Yet concerns about the long-term outlook for fuel demand remain, especially in Asia. The conflict has also exposed the need for buyers to diversify supplies.
For decades, consumers, refiners and producers organised investments around access to the cheapest, largest reservoirs of oil and gas, often treating energy security as a secondary consideration.

That balance is shifting. Buyers shaken by months of disruptions are increasingly willing to pay a premium for reliable supplies, while producers are reassessing the value of geographic diversification.

For international oil companies, this strengthens the case for directing capital towards new producing regions such as the Atlantic Basin, Africa and Asia rather than concentrating investment in the Middle East.
Companies are, therefore, beginning to accelerate development of existing oil and gas assets while increasing exploration spending in countries such as Namibia, Brazil, Angola and Venezuela.
Competition for resources outside the Middle East is thus likely to intensify.

The challenge will be ensuring new projects remain profitable in what is likely to be a much lower-price environment in the future — even as firms face rising costs today for rigs, equipment and skilled labour.

In recent years, major oil companies have targeted average break-even costs of roughly US$40 a barrel for new developments, but that figure will likely rise in the coming years due to inflationary pressures.
Finally, the conflict has reshaped global trade flows.

As Asian buyers increasingly source crude oil and liquefied natural gas from the Atlantic Basin, voyage times have more than doubled compared with traditional Middle Eastern routes, pushing tanker rates to record highs as supply chains stretch.
What initially appeared to be a temporary adjustment is increasingly becoming a structural feature of global energy markets.
For companies with large trading businesses, including Shell and BP, longer supply chains could justify greater investment in tankers, storage facilities and trading infrastructure.

For now, investors still welcome greater returns in the form of dividends and share repurchases. But, over time, Big Oil will need to put forward a clear vision for how it will navigate this altered environment.
The winners of the next decade will not be the energy companies that merely harvest today's windfall profits.
They will be those that use them to prepare for a world of higher geopolitical risk, longer supply chains and a global push for energy security.
The writer is from Reuters

5711a1bca2813581: AS if there are not enough things to worry parents of school-going children, the subject of school bullies is among the most vexing they have to confront.
If there is one thing that will give parents ease of mind when sending their children to school, it is the certainty that bullies are yesterday's problem.
Unfortunately, it is not, especially in boarding schools.

But parents have received a welcome double dose of good news, firstly, with the latest government pronouncement that closed-circuit television (CCTV) camera coverage will be extended to 333 boarding schools this year, thus ensuring 24-hour monitoring and surveillance against violence perpetrated by students on their peers.

The additional good news is that former military personnel will be hired as full-time wardens in all 58 Mara Junior Science Colleges (MRSM) from next year to curb bullying and other discipline issues in college hostels.
This follows from the success of a pilot project at MRSM Besut and MRSM Balik Pulau, where bullying cases dropped to nearly zero after former military personnel were deployed.

These encouraging developments are not isolated moves but point to the prioritisation of safety in schools as an institutional issue requiring all-out efforts aimed at prevention, supervision, deterrence and early intervention.
While CCTV monitor-ing obviously helps, there is nothing like the physical presence of dedicated wardens to provide what technology alone cannot.
These personnel can spot tensions before they get out of control and intervene early. Mere monitoring to ensure tensions do not boil over into violent incidents is not enough.
Prevention is always better than cure and the only way to identify warning signs and discourage misconduct before it escalates is often through the presence of minders.

Technology complements but cannot replace human supervision. CCTVs are only useful if footage is properly and constantly monitored, incidents are acted upon quickly and any blind spots are immediately addressed.
Unfortunately, discipline matters also cannot be solved by a tough, on-site presence alone. Bullying has morphed from physical abuse to verbal, psychological and even digital abuse.

Vigilance and supervision have to be accordingly all-encompassing as well. The wider lesson is accountability. Parents must be confident complaints will be heard, investigated promptly and appropriate action taken, while students also need safe channels to report bullying.
Overall, the latest moves point in a most welcome direction. More CCTV cameras and wardens are, however, not the be-all and end-all.
The government should circulate and regularly review performance indicators such as prevalence of bullying reports, repeat incidents, response times and student and parent feedback.
The ultimate measure of success will be when bullying no longer plagues schools and they become known solely as redoubts for learning and building character.

7c2589dc49585f41: PETALING JAYA: This weekend’s Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia has been declared a heat-hazard race, with temperatures expected to reach up to 33°C during the event.
According to the BBC, the designation is the third heat-hazard classification of the season, following the Austrian and Italian grands prix.
A heat hazard is an official status given to a race when temperatures are forecast to exceed 31°C at some point during the event.
Temperatures are forecast to range between 31°C and 33°C throughout the race weekend, with high humidity and a chance of rain each day.
The race is being held in Malaysia as a replacement for the Bahrain Grand Prix, which was postponed from its original April date because of the war in the Middle East.

The heat-hazard classification allows drivers to use an in-car cooling system that circulates a cooled liquid, such as glycol, through pipes in a fireproof top worn underneath their overalls. The cooling kit is optional.
However, drivers who choose not to use it must carry 5kg of ballast in their cars to ensure they do not gain a competitive advantage.
The designation was first introduced last year after technology for the cooling vest had been developed.
Some drivers have opted not to use the cooling system because of discomfort and concerns that the coolant could run out before the race ends.
If that happens, the liquid can reach the temperature of the car, which is considerably higher than the ambient temperature.
Cockpit temperatures in an F1 car can exceed 40°C, while drivers wear several layers of fireproof clothing in addition to a balaclava and helmet.
The combination makes overheating a significant concern during races held in extreme heat.

6ac1fca4a8a0d65f: If you've always wanted to say you have "people" to attend your meetings, there's an app in development for that, as long as you're comfortable with the idea of eventually sending an AI bot in your place and potentially offending your human colleagues. MeetTwins, from Indian developer Aditya Shinde, is an AI assistant currently recruiting users for its beta. It's designed for a single purpose: to attend Google Meet calls on behalf of its operator and relay approved information to colleagues without requiring its human to spend precious time actually speaking to coworkers. Shinde describes the tool on its website as being inspired by his own desire to send an AI bot to his Google Meet calls, an idea he instead decided to develop into an actual product built using AI models from India-based AI firm Sarvam, and with the ability to add a digital twin avatar created by Simli. Use cases described on MeetTwins' website include status update meetings, students who have to juggle work with class, and even sales and customer teams who need to handle routine check-in calls with clients, though we don't advise that for businesses who want their customers to feel like they care about them. Prepping MeetTwins for a call involves telling it what questions to answer, providing documents or files participants may request, and supplying other context it may need. Certain topics can be designated off limits for the discussion as well. Shinde told The Register in a LinkedIn conversation that it’s solely designed to answer questions that were approved by its user, and that it won’t guess, make anything up, or promise something that a human ought to have final say on. “If a prospect asks something that isn't covered in the brief, MeetTwins will not try to improvise,” Shinde told us. Anything outside the defined realm of discussion is instead referred to MeetTwins’ operator, who receives an email after the call summarizing the things that were discussed and any open items to address. Let’s be frank for a moment: No one wants to be stuck in a boring Google Meet call that could have been an email – an argument for which MeetTwins, ironically, provides even further justification – but deciding to send an AI representative on your behalf isn’t likely to engender feelings of camaraderie or support from one’s coworkers. Shinde admitted he’s aware of that and has built features into MeetTwins to account for that very situation. “We are very conscious of this,” Shinde noted. “If anyone in the meeting is uncomfortable, they can simply type "/stop" in the chat, and MeetTwins will leave immediately.” In other words, there’s a distinct possibility that colleagues upset they had to engage with an AI instead of their coworker will simply eject the bot and send a grumpy email after the meeting asking for whatever information you were going to provide, potentially CC’ing a supervisor on that note, too. Shinde said that clearly labeling the MeetTwins bot as an AI in the call, and announcing it when it first speaks, "actually builds trust,” though we imagine that might not be the case with those who are skeptical of AI. A good use of AI? That’s up for debate, but it does prove one thing: We’re all wasting a lot of time in virtual meetings that could probably just be an email or a Slack message - preferably one penned by an actual human whose busy schedule might not have any spare time. ®

7abd4d2d77e4231c: AI-based tools seem to be causing security threats on a nearly daily basis, in part because we've been slow to recognize potential threats. One area where we seem to be ahead of the game, however, is in biosecurity.

As with most things biological, utility goes hand in hand with threats. We've developed increasingly sophisticated tools for designing proteins and seen some major successes, such as AI-designed enzymes that can digest plastics or block venom proteins. 05e8432107d40731: The AI industry must generate $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031 to keep funding the infrastructure needed to meet anticipated demand, and this will require imaginative new uses beyond simply enhancing employee productivity. That $6 trillion figure comes from the 2026 annual Global Technology Report from management consultants Bain & Company, which put its thinking cap on to figure out how the AI sector can possibly meet this challenge. It says the massive demand for AI compute infrastructure has revived the hardware industry. Some of the fastest growing segments include high-bandwidth memory (HBM) used in GPUs, advanced packaging and custom silicon, and application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) all scaling rapidly. As The Register reported last year, AI spending is actually keeping the US economy out of recession, with datacenter infrastructure and model development providing the only significant growth areas. Bain points to the “arms race” among hyperscalers for AI capacity, claiming that capital expenditure by Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, and Oracle could hit $780 billion for the whole of 2026, nearly five times the level seen just three years earlier. By 2031, it estimates that annual spending on AI infrastructure could reach $1.5 trillion, a figure that is not far off the $1.6 trillion forecast separately by analyst firm Omdia. The $6 trillion comes from the Bain's assumption that capital expenditure will amount to about 25 percent of industry revenue, an ambitious but reasonable percentage based on trends among cloud providers, it says. Bain expects that existing applications of AI will grow, but estimates these will add up to a total between $1.2 trillion and $1.8 trillion in revenue. This includes consumer AI, via subscriptions and advertisements, plus enterprise AI, through software development, sales, marketing, customer service, and IT operations. That leaves a remaining $4.2 trillion of additional revenue for the industry to find from somewhere. Four possible categories emerge from Bain’s research as possibilities to fill this gap. It says that AI models are replacing search engines and integrating ads to generate new revenue, which means the developers could unlock $100 billion to $200 billion of extra cash. Secondly, AI to make autonomous cars, trucks, and drones, as well as other industrial automation, could create new products and services worth about $400 billion, Basin estimates. A similar category is physical AI, in which category it includes simulations, digital twins, and robotics, with a calculated worth of as much as $900 billion. Those three add up to $1.5 trillion, leaving Bain with a $2.7 trillion shortfall. What could make up the rest of the AI industry revenue? It puts forward “new products and uses that don’t exist today,” which is the kind of answer that your granny could have come up with. In this category it stuffs AI-driven drug discovery, mental health support that might address billions of dollars in unmet demand, materials science breakthroughs in areas such as battery technology and semiconductors, and accelerating scientific research in fields from neuroscience to fusion energy. “The debate today is fixated on employee productivity. The economics of AI infrastructure demand trillions in new revenue beyond productivity gains. What the industry needs is a wave of innovation that will dwarf what mobile and cloud unlocked,” said David Crawford, chairman of Bain’s global Technology practice. It is only a year since a previous report of Bain’s forecast that the industry would need to hit $2 trillion in revenue by 2030 to keep feeding the infrastructure beast. That figure has now trebled, which is perhaps an indication of just how much the investment going into AI has ballooned over the past 12 months. There are reasons to think the AI industry is not going to hit $6 trillion in annual revenue by 2031. The Register has published numerous reports indicating that AI rollouts are just not paying off, such as this one, this one or this one. At the same time, doubts are being cast over whether all those AI infrastructure projects will be realized. A report from investment bank Jefferies found only half the US datacenter capacity scheduled for 2026 is actually under construction and work is yet to begin on as much as 80 percent of the 2028 pipeline. Another report from the same company suggested that chip manufacturing constraints will limit how many planned AI server farms can be brought online over the next several years. ®
08cae46ecd1dd21c: MELAKA: The immigration department has arrested a housewife suspected of impersonating a senior immigration officer and offering services to process work pass applications for foreigners.

“When she was detained at the cafe, the suspect was dealing with a Chinese national who claimed to have paid about RM6,000 to obtain a work permit,” he said at a press conference here today.
Anirwan said the suspect offered services to apply for work passes for foreigners or temporary visit passes for employment without the employers or foreigners having to visit an immigration office.

A preliminary investigation found that the suspect had been operating alone for one to two years. She allegedly targeted employers or foreigners who appeared desperate to obtain work permits, he said.
He said the mother of five had also uploaded pictures of herself wearing the department’s uniform on social media to convince employers that she was an immigration officer.
The suspect has been remanded for four days from today to assist in the investigation under Sections 56(1)(k) and 56(1)(l) of the Immigration Act 1959/63.

e06e3480cbac54a1: PUTRAJAYA: The Audi Revolut F1 Team driver Gabriel Bortoleto is hoping for rain during the Formula 1 (F1) Bahrain Grand Prix (GP) at the Sepang International Circuit (SIC) in Sepang, on Oct 2-4.

ef003b4bbba4d85e: MELAKA: Jabatan Imigresen Melaka menahan seorang wanita tempatan yang disyaki menyamar sebagai pegawai kanan Imigresen dan menjadi dalang menguruskan permohonan pas kerja bagi warga asing yang ingin mendapatkan permit bekerja di negara ini.

"Suspek menawarkan khidmat permohonan pas kerja bagi warga asing yang memerlukan permit kerja atau pas lawatan kerja sementara tanpa majikan atau warga asing terlibat perlu hadir ke pejabat Imigresen," katanya pada sidang akhbar.

Turut hadir, Timbalan Pengarah Imigresen Melaka (Kawalan) merangkap Ketua Bahagian Penguatkuasaan Jabatan Imigresen Melaka Suzila Suhya dan Ketua Unit Risik dan Operasi Jabatan Imigresen Melaka Irwan Rizalman Abd Rashid.

Beliau berkata, ibu kepada lima anak itu turut memuat naik gambarnya yang lengkap berpakaian seragam jabatan itu di media sosial bagi meyakinkan majikan bahawa suspek merupakan anggota jabatan itu.

Anirwan Fauzee berkata, suspek direman empat hari bermula hari ini bagi membantu siasatan di bawah Seksyen 56(1)(k) dan Seksyen 56(1)(l) Akta Imigresen 1959/63 kerana cubaan memperoleh secara membuat kenyataan palsu atau tanpa kuasa yang sah mempunyai dalam milikannya pas, dokumen atau perakuan yang palsu atau yang dipinda secara menyalahi undang-undang.
"Jabatan Imigresen Melaka turut mengeluarkan saman saksi kepada mangsa atau pelanggan dan suami suspek bagi membantu siasatan lanjut," katanya.

"Sehubungan itu, orang awam dinasihatkan sentiasa berwaspada dan tidak mudah terpedaya dengan individu yang menawarkan perkhidmatan Imigresen secara tidak rasmi, sebaliknya berurusan terus di pejabat Jabatan Imigresen terdekat."
ae406487a126b251: KUALA LUMPUR: Bahrain will showcase its cultural heritage, cuisine and entertainment to motorsport fans in Asia through The Bahrain Village and other off-track attractions at the Formula 1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix Malaysia 2026, which will be held at the Sepang International Circuit (SIC) from Friday to Sunday.

4804c9a1d7621ba0: MILWAUKEE: G20 trade ministers began talks Wednesday in the US with President Donald Trump's global tariffs casting a pall over the gathering, pushing countries to seek cooperation outside the world's biggest economy.
Officials from the Group of 20 major economies – which includes China, India, Russia, Japan, Canada and France – are holding two days of intensive talks and bilateral meetings in Milwaukee.
But their gathering in the Midwestern city comes amid a deepening US-Canada trade war, waves of US tariffs and Trump's investigations into member countries over excess industrial capacity.
Analysts expect few breakthroughs as trade tensions simmer. China rejects worries about its exports and criticism of overcapacity, seen as unfairly driving down prices by flooding markets.
Countries are meanwhile seeking deals with the Trump administration as top US trade official Jamieson Greer hosts his counterparts, with India pushing to get its trade pact over the finish line.
The G20 trade ministerial comes after finance ministers met in Asheville, setting the stage for a December leaders' summit in Miami.
Heading into talks early Wednesday, Polish finance minister Andrzej Domanski urged for a lowering of trade barriers.
"Our position was always very clear: That tariffs are bad for companies, are bad for customers and of course are increasing inflation," he told reporters.
"I do hope that our US partners will stick to all settlements that were made," he added, referring to an earlier deal between the US and EU to cap Trump's duties on the bloc at 15%.
Poland is not a permanent G20 member but has been invited to the table this year as Washington holds the grouping's rotating presidency. In turn, US officials have excluded South Africa.
Also on the agenda this week are efforts to eliminate forced labour in supply chains and the targeting of access to food supplies to pressure others.
Domanski on Wednesday condemned "all actions taken by Russia against the export of agriculture products from Ukraine," as Moscow and Kyiv remain at war after Russia's 2022 invasion.
Tariff threats
Domanski's remarks come as US investigations into overcapacity target 16 trading partners including China, the EU, Japan and India.
This brings the threat of further tariffs even on partners that have struck tariff deals with Washington, like the EU and Japan.
Greer maintained at a roundtable late Tuesday that the United States "is not anti-trade."
Asked about existing deals to cut tariffs imposed by Trump in his second presidency, Greer told reporters Tuesday: "We will certainly take them into account."
On striking a pact with Canada, where certain products now face a US ban due to their trade spat, Greer added: "It's not urgent for us."
"At some point will there be a deal? I mean, presumably, they have to trade with us a lot. We trade a lot with them too."
"Eventually, it will happen," he said.
Under pressure
Even as G20 officials want to cooperate with the US, "they will also be under pressure to voice their concerns with tariffs," former US trade official Wendy Cutler told AFP.
Cutler, now with the Asia Society Policy Institute, expects some countries will "mince no words" as they feel they have been unfairly targeted on excess capacity.
Trump has unleashed a barrage of tariffs on trading partners since returning to the White House, separately targeting sectors like steel and autos.
While the Supreme Court struck down many of his duties, US officials have reimposed new tariffs on 60 partners – covering most trade – by alleging insufficient action against forced labour.
Canada's international trade minister Maninder Sidhu stressed Ottawa's support for "open, predictable and rules-based trade" ahead of Wednesday's talks.
He plans to speak with partners in Milwaukee as Canadian officials try to diversify an economy they view as too reliant on an increasingly protectionist United States.
The G20 comprises 19 nations plus the EU and the African Union.
d7d2ae7ce823d582: SEPANG: Motorcyclists are prohibited from entering the Sepang International Circuit (SIC) area during the Formula 1 (F1) Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix (GP), which takes place this weekend.
SIC chief executive officer Azhan Shafriman Hanif said this was part of a new traffic management plan with the Royal Malaysia Police (PDRM) to ensure smooth traffic flow for visitors.

He said that since the circuit began operations 27 years ago, unrestricted access to all types of vehicles had proven to be the major cause of severe traffic congestion every time a mega motor sports event was held.
"From 1999 until now, we have not been very strategic in terms of traffic control as we allowed all vehicles to enter, resulting in heavy traffic flow and congestion in and out of the circuit.

"So, this time we are restricting private vehicles and prohibiting members of the public from entering the SIC on motorcycles to reduce congestion, while making it easier for police to control traffic," he told a media conference here today.
Azhan Shafriman said only vehicles with valid parking stickers or passes would be allowed through the checkpoints and into the circuit's parking area.
For those without parking passes, he suggested that they make use of public transport, e-hailing services and the free shuttle buses provided throughout the race weekend.

He said 115 free shuttle buses would be provided through a collaboration with Rapid KL at four strategic locations, namely Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) Terminal 2, KLIA Long-Term Car Park (LCTP), Mitsui Outlet Park and Bandar Enstek.
"In addition to the 115 buses at the four external hubs, SIC is also providing 30 free shuttle buses within the circuit, which will operate non-stop from 7 am to midnight," he added.

0340737932052eda: PETALING JAYA: A former DAP MP has challenged the home minister to furnish proof that Myanmar nationals are a “financial burden” or a “security threat”.

The group is the first of 5,000 Myanmar nationals Malaysia says have agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centres.
Santiago also questioned if the Myanmar nationals were more of a threat than the two million undocumented migrant workers who have arrived in the country in the last 20 years.

72a569e198250722: BANGKOK: About 8,000 pieces of baggage remain stranded at Bangkok's Suvarnabhumi Airport after flooding disrupted airport operations, with authorities expecting to clear the backlog within three to four days as additional personnel are deployed.

Deputy Prime Minister and Transport Minister Phiphat Ratchakitprakarn said Thai Airways International could sort and clear up to 2,000 pieces of baggage a day when operating at full capacity.
He said about 1,800 pieces had since been cleared and returned to passengers, leaving around 8,000 awaiting processing.
"Thai Airways is working to clear the backlog of both baggage and passengers, particularly transit passengers, who still make up a large number," he told reporters at Suvarnabhumi Airport.
Phiphat said the government has mobilised additional support, with the Royal Thai Air Force deploying 100 personnel to assist with lifting, transporting and other baggage-handling operations.
He said baggage sorting would remain with Thai Airways personnel as it required specialised expertise, while military personnel would focus mainly on lifting and transportation.

"Baggage sorting requires specific skills and expertise. Therefore, we are adding manpower to assist with lifting and transportation so that Thai Airways staff can focus fully on tasks requiring their expertise," he said.

Meanwhile, Thai Airways has temporarily suspended inbound, outbound and transit cargo acceptance at its Suvarnabhumi cargo terminal from Sept 30 to Oct 6 as flooding continues to disrupt staff travel and warehouse operations.

b2b5f55ded4b0590: NAGOYA: China's divers extended their remarkable Asian Games unbeaten record stretching back to 1974 as a top Japanese official apologised Wednesday for "inconveniences" that have dogged the continent's premier sporting event.
Chinese divers were unstoppable once more as the country's massive overall tally of gold medals swelled to 150 with four days left.
Hosts Japan are a distant second with 50 golds, ahead of South Korea with 24.

China has won every diving gold medal since their first Asian Games appearance 52 years ago.
"Girls are every bit as capable as boys. We are pushing ourselves to perform more difficult dives, too," said Chen, a double Paris Olympics champion.
"We do not train any less than the boys," she added.
In tennis, Philippines star Alexandra Eala stormed into the semi-finals, cheered on by fans who had come from far and wide to see their hero in action.

"Representing my country and playing these types of games, SEA Games, Asian Games and hopefully the Olympics, they're very close to my heart and a big part of my dreams," said Eala.

- 'Mishandling' -
Nagoya's mayor apologised to athletes for "inconveniences" at the Games following a string of complaints.
The event has been marred by problems including a shortage of beds and issues with transport.
There are over 17,000 athletes and officials, more than the Olympics, and countries have accused local organisers of mismanagement.
"We must offer our apologies to the athletes and others affected by these inconveniences," said Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa, who is also acting chairman of the local organising committee.
"We must sincerely reflect on the mishandling that occurred," he added.
Unlike past Games, there is no athletes' village in a bid to save money, with participants instead sleeping in temporary wooden units, on a cruise ship and in hotels.
- Sleep-deprived -
With days of rain finally giving way to warm sunshine in Nagoya, Tom Kim defied jet-lag and just six hours' sleep in two days to shoot a three-under par 67 as the golf began.

"I've had six hours of sleep in the last 48 so I'm hanging in there," Kim, a four-time US PGA Tour winner, told AFP.
Taichi Kho, the defending champion, had a hole-in-one in his round of one-under par 69.-AFP

1205b0fdc4b7b105: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia is seeing a surge in travel interest ahead of the Formula 1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix at the Sepang International Circuit, with accommodation searches for Kuala Lumpur, Sepang and surrounding areas jumping more than 160 per cent year-on-year.

Bae Jun-ho was their hero, ghosting in at the back post to head in a dramatic 82nd-minute winner at Nagai Stadium.
"We were expecting a challenging match, but we persevered," said South Korea coach Lee Min-sung.
"We conceded first to make it even harder, but our team fought back, and I'm happy with that."
Lee's side are attempting to bring some cheer to South Korean football fans after a disappointing World Cup that saw the senior team exit in the group stage.
China's men have never won Asian Games football gold and were contesting their first semi-final since 1998.
History looked on the cards when Wang Yudong finished off a smart team move with an emphatic finish to put China ahead on 22 minutes.

In an entertaining encounter in front of a sparse crowd, Lee Young-jun hit back for South Korea 11 minutes later with China goalkeeper Li Hao getting a hand to his header but unable to keep the ball out.
Both sides had chances in the second half, before Stoke City's Bae popped up with the winner.
China coach Antonio Puche will now have to rally his men with a bronze medal on the line against Uzbekistan.
"I spoke with the players and what I said is that even though we lost, the important thing was that we fought," he said.
"We lost, but we are proud."

9f49b513f8de7ed3: Google.org announced on Sept. 15 that the MIT Transit Lab is a recipient of $2.1 million in funding — one of only 15 projects selected in the worldwide Google.org Impact Challenge: AI for Government Innovation. The funding from Google’s philanthropic arm will support NGOs, social enterprises, and academic institutions as they integrate artificial intelligence-powered solutions across topics like health, resilience, and economy. The Transit Lab’s winning project, the Public Transit Intelligence Hub (PTIQ), aims to unify public transportation agencies’ real-time monitoring, operations control, and passenger communication systems into a single centralized AI-orchestrated platform that will allow transit control center staff to make better-informed, on-the-spot decisions, and provide riders with more immediate and accurate information. The control centers of public transportation agencies are similar in appearance to the portrayal of NASA mission control in movies: rooms filled with employees monitoring dozens of radio feeds and computer screens relaying real-time camera data about stations and their operations, transit vehicle locations, riders, traffic, and road conditions. Unfortunately, the information coming in is fragmented, rather than integrated into a centralized system with overall awareness of the network’s conditions. This system creates an intense work environment for the transit staff making operations and communications decisions that can affect thousands of passengers relying on transit to get them where they need to go. “Public transportation agencies are required to make decisions around the clock regarding real-time operations, control, and passenger communication,” says Awad Abdelhalim, associate director of the Transit Lab, and PTIQ co-principal investigator, project director, and technical lead. “Our goal isn't to automate those decisions, but to make sure the people making them have the best information possible. By unifying and streamlining data and information flow from fragmented and siloed internal systems, PTIQ will improve the experience of both riders and the transit workforce.” Jinhua Zhao, the MIT Class of 1941 Professor of City and Transportation, head of the MIT Department of Urban Studies and Planning, and founder and director of the MIT Mobility Initiative (MMI), is the other co-principal investigator on the project. The PTIQ program manager is MIT Lecturer Jim Aloisi, who directs the Transit Research Consortium, which will also work on the project. That consortium is comprised of researchers from the Transit Lab, MMI, and Northeastern University, where Professor Haris Koutsopoulos takes the lead.  In addition to providing funding for the three-year project, Google.org will provide pro bono support from its own engineers and AI product experts. "AI holds incredible potential to transform public services, but there is often a gap between promise and practice,” says Maggie Johnson, global head of Google.org. “By equipping the 15 selected organizations with funding and pro bono support from Google's own AI experts, we are empowering the people closest to the problem to show what is truly possible. Together, we can ensure that AI makes a profound, positive difference in the everyday lives of communities worldwide." The project will build on the group’s decades of experience in applied-research collaborations with transit agencies in major metropolitan areas throughout the world. PTIQ’s decision support interface for control center staff will integrate predictive models, optimization engines, and large language model-based contextual reasoning. But ultimately the decision-making based on that information will be left to transit staff, who can better balance the trade-offs of making one decision over another in these often incredibly complex situations. “The hard part of integrating AI in transit is not the technology; it’s the institution,” Zhao says. “AI is evaluated on benchmarks. Public transit is assessed in the control center and on the streets. Over decades of work with transit agencies in Washington, D.C., Chicago, London, Boston, Tokyo, and Hong Kong, we have learned to ask a different question. Not whether AI can do this, but whether it can work in the organization and whether the staff trust it. PTIQ is designed to ground AI in the institutional reality and behavioral nuances of a transit agency, and bring machine intelligence and human judgment into one place.” “Currently the evaluation of AI models relies heavily on deterministic, objective tasks, such as solving mathematical equations or generating code,” Abdelhalim explains. “However, the vast majority of real-world operational tasks — like delivering public transit services — are highly dynamic, multi-stakeholder, and lack a single correct objective answer. These complex spatiotemporal environments are the ultimate testbed for evaluating what AI systems can add to society.” PTIQ aims to transform the transit workforce experience, the transit rider experience, and the overall ability of transit agencies to efficiently respond to disruptions and unexpected events.  “We expect that PTIQ will take what is largely a siloed environment and connect it in ways that provide powerful benefits for the agency workforce and its riders,” says Aloisi, who is also a former secretary of transportation for the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. “[Doing this by] improving response time, reducing platform and bus stop crowding, providing riders with higher quality and timely information, and supporting agency staff — from dispatchers to vehicle operators and communications staff — with high-quality, reliable, real-time information and solution sets.”

4425dae96bc6ed42: For a few years now, the PS5 hacking community has been chipping away at various exploits that let users fully jailbreak their locked-down console. For the most part, though, those exploits have only worked with years-old versions of the PS5's frequently updated firmware, making them less than useful for many everyday users.

That changed Tuesday with the release of the new Relapse exploit, which works with any PS5 up to firmware version 13.6 (released in July). That means jailbreaking is now possible on any PS5 that was last updated before the mid-September release of firmware version 14.00.00.

The so-called Relapse exploit makes use of a long-known WebKit vulnerability in the PS5's hard-to-access web browser, escalating from there to gain write access to the PS5 kernel and install an ELF loader to streamline the running of arbitrary code. The new method is also a lot more efficient than previous PS5 jailbreak exploits, which could hang the system for 50 minutes per attempt.
688e41d4f6dd51d2: A former National Crime Agency (NCA) officer who stole Bitcoin seized during an investigation into Silk Road 2.0 has been ordered to hand over more than £1.8 million ($2.4 million). Paul Chowles, 44, stole 50 of the 97 Bitcoin recovered from convicted Silk Road 2.0 administrator Thomas White. Police later recovered 30 of the stolen coins. US and European authorities shut down Silk Road 2.0 in November 2014 as part of an international operation targeting dark web marketplaces. The 50 Bitcoin were worth about £60,000 ($79,000) when Chowles stole them in 2017. Chowles had worked on the NCA investigation into criminal activity on the original Silk Road and later took the lead in analyzing data and extracting cryptocurrency from devices seized from White. Between May 6 and 7, 2017, he transferred 50 Bitcoin from White's "retirement wallet" to an address under his control. He then divided the coins into smaller amounts and routed them through Bitcoin Fog, a mixing service used to obscure cryptocurrency transactions. By the time of his sentencing in July 2025, the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) valued the 50 Bitcoin at more than £4.4 million ($5.8 million). The CPS said the rise in Bitcoin's value helped take the benefit attributed to Chowles' offending to £1,970,759.27. When making a confiscation order, a court considers both the benefit obtained through the crime and the defendant's "available amount" – the value of assets that can be used to satisfy the order. Chowles' available amount was assessed at £1,810,678.93, and Liverpool Crown Court ordered him to pay that sum. Luke Clements, specialist prosecutor at the CPS Proceeds of Crime Division, said: "Paul Chowles exploited a position of trust for personal gain, stealing assets that had already been recovered through law enforcement action. "Confiscation orders are a powerful tool in ensuring that crime does not pay. Today's order sends a clear message that we will pursue offenders' assets relentlessly and seek to recover criminal proceeds wherever they are hidden. "The CPS Proceeds of Crime Division will continue to work closely with law enforcement partners to identify criminal benefit and take robust action to strip offenders of the profits of their crimes." Chowles, from Bristol, was dismissed from the NCA on July 11, 2025. Five days later, Liverpool Crown Court sentenced him to five years and six months in prison after he pleaded guilty to theft, transferring criminal property, and concealing criminal property. Suspicion eventually fell on Chowles after White insisted that someone inside the NCA must have taken the Bitcoin. The NCA initially assumed White had moved the missing Bitcoin himself because he had the technical knowledge to do so. By late 2021, investigators regarded the coins as untraceable and wrote them off. Following White's conviction, the court imposed a confiscation order of £1,560,506. The NCA sold the remaining 47 Bitcoin to satisfy part of it, leaving £1,066,956 outstanding. White maintained that someone within the agency had stolen the other 50 coins because NCA investigators held the private keys to his wallet. Merseyside Police was responsible for managing White locally after his release on license in early 2022. When Merseyside officers met NCA counterparts to discuss White's allegation, Chowles attended the meeting. Merseyside Police subsequently opened an investigation and arrested him in May 2022. Investigators recovered an iPhone linking Chowles to an account used to transfer Bitcoin, along with relevant searches for a cryptocurrency exchange. They also found notebooks in his office containing usernames, passwords, and statements relating to White's cryptocurrency accounts. ®

999d38bb2f014b77: MADRID: Spanish prime minister Pedro Sanchez on Wednesday said he was "reasonably optimistic" that parliament would approve housing measures his minority government adopted after nationwide protests sparked by a Madrid pensioner's eviction.

Last week's eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal catalysed long-running anger about runaway housing costs and thrust the issue to the forefront of national politics ahead of a general election next year.
But Sanchez's Socialist-led coalition faces the arduous task of convincing enough parties in a heavily fragmented parliament to pass two decrees on Friday.
"I am reasonably optimistic about the validation," Sanchez said about his government's decrees during a joint press conference in Madrid with French President Emmanuel Macron.
A standout measure is a ban until the end of 2030 on evicting tenants deemed vulnerable and who have no alternative housing, a scenario raised by Abascal's case.
Any tenant – even if not deemed vulnerable – with no alternative accommodation but whose property is owned by a company identified as a "vulture fund" will also be protected from eviction.
The government also seeks to ban until the end of 2028 the acquisition of properties by companies with "speculative" aims, a demand of the protesters who regularly denounce "vulture funds".
The legislation defines them as companies which acquire real estate or portfolios of unpaid mortgage loans at prices below 70 percent of the market value with a view to maximising profit afterwards.
The automatic renewal of tenant contracts, another key demand of protesters, is also included but is viewed by analysts as harder to pass.
The main opposition conservative Popular Party (PP), the largest group in parliament, has announced it will reject the measures, while the support of a host of small formations is unclear.
Sanchez lashed out at PP criticism of his housing policy, saying he "liked being a traitor" to "vulture funds and those who speculate with housing".

The Socialist premier, accused of failing to contain housing prices since taking office in 2018, said, "We have made an enormous negotiating effort" and called on parliament to approve the decrees as a "question of humanity".

84d5959095fa4c9f: Old-fashioned striped barbershop poles turn in place on a vertical axis, but humans typically perceive the stripes moving upward rather than turning with the pole. It's a well-known visual illusion arising from processing biases in human vision. According to a new paper published in the journal Nature, a similar effect could explain how butterflies often evade predatory birds: Their flight patterns and wing patterns combine to make it hard for predators to accurately gauge speed and direction.

"The stripes and spots on many butterflies’ wings interfere with the way visual systems try to guess the direction and speed of moving things, boosting false motion cues while hiding the butterfly's true heading," said co-author George Hancock of the University of Exeter in Cornwall. "The illusions interfere with the predator’s most basic visual targeting system and disrupt the final ‘ballistic attack’ in the tens of milliseconds when it commits to grabbing its prey, with no time to change course. As a result, birds and other predators will often simply miss."

Butterfly wings have long fascinated scientists, ever since the first documentation of the growth of said wings back in 1938. By 2021, researchers at MIT had captured on video the unique structural growth of butterfly wings—continuously, as a butterfly develops inside its chrysalis—for the very first time. Butterfly wings are an example of structural color in nature: the bright iridescent colors don’t come from pigment molecules but from what physicists call photonic crystals. The scales of chitin (a polysaccharide common to insects) are arranged like roof tiles. Essentially, they form a diffraction grating, except photonic crystals only produce certain colors, or wavelengths, of light, while a diffraction grating will produce the entire spectrum.

19e64cc957db4421: There are two boundaries around any AI system in a regulated industry, and they have different owners. One is the jurisdiction: what data can leave the country, and under whose rules. The other is the building: what can leave your own estate at all, and who signs for it when it does. Most AI programs do not stall on the model. They stall here, on where the data lives, who can reach it, and what an auditor will accept as evidence twelve months from now. The proprietary data that makes an AI system worth building is the same data that makes it a risk to build. And the boundary drawn around a pilot has a habit of quietly becoming the boundary around production, whether or not anyone chose it. A product sheet does not answer those questions. They get answered case by case, with a particular regulator and a particular legal team in the room, which is why The Register is putting them to HPE and NVIDIA over dinner in Washington on Thursday 29 October. Editor-in-chief Matt Rosoff takes the chair and nothing is on the record. HPE sends Thierry Pienaar, HPE Fellow and Chief Technology Officer for HPC and AI Worldwide Sales. NVIDIA sends Bert Condensa, Vice President for Enterprise AI Factory Segment Sales. Both are there to take questions. Nobody is bringing slides, and the chair cuts off anyone who starts pitching. The evening runs under the Chatham House Rule, so what is said can be used and who said it cannot. That is what makes the useful answers possible, like what a hospital group’s legal team refused to sign, and what it signed instead. On the table: which infrastructure options actually hold a boundary, what each one costs in capital, in capability or in elasticity, and whether any of it survives the move from planning into running operations. The table is for technology, data and risk leaders in healthcare, financial services, research, pharmaceuticals, government and higher education who are making these calls now rather than next year. Dinner runs from 6.00pm to 8.30pm at Fiola Mare. Places are limited and go by invitation. Request one here. ea039df066f8591e: A new AI system that excels at challenging games with hidden information could someday help human decision-makers select ideal strategies to outfox opponents in complicated situations like military maneuvers. Using advances in machine-learning, researchers from MIT, Carnegie Mellon University, New York University, and Stanford University developed an AI that defeated top-ranked human players of the board wargame Stratego by a large margin — something no AI system had been able to achieve.  Stratego, a two-player game of imperfect information, in which the opponent’s piece identities remain hidden, is often used as a benchmark to test the strategic thinking abilities of powerful AI models. To build their model, the researchers combined efficient training algorithms with new techniques tailored for calculated decision-making in hidden information settings.  The AI system achieved greater performance at Stratego than the next best models, while being far cheaper and less computationally demanding to train. The system also outperformed top human players in other strategic games with different rules and designs, demonstrating how it can be generalized for a variety of use-cases. The AI system could be adapted to help humans tackle many real-world problems with hidden information, such as business negotiations or cybersecurity.  “In the kind of imperfect information tasks you would face in reality, you often don’t have the luxury of enumerating through all the possibilities. There are just too many. Having AI algorithms that are general purpose and can provably perform this challenging task so well is a big step forward,” says Gabriele Farina, an assistant professor in the Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS), principal investigator at the Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS), and senior author of a paper on this AI system. He is joined on the paper by lead author Samuel Sokota, a graduate student at Carnegie Mellon; Eugene Vinitsky, an assistant professor at NYU; Zico Kolter, a professor at Carnegie Mellon; Hengyuan Hu, a graduate student at Stanford; and Zhiyuan Fan, an EECS graduate student at MIT. The research appears today in Nature. Hidden information The world is full of imperfect information problems.  In these interactions, some parties possess information others do not. For instance, traders in financial markets may not know the rationale behind the trades of others, while military forces likely don’t have full knowledge of enemy positions.  With hidden information, the decisions parties make, as well as the decisions they choose not to make, are intertwined in such a way that it is extremely difficult to determine the best steps to take next. “The more you bluff, the more your opponent expects it, and the less each bluff is worth. It’s not obvious how to reason about that,” Sokota explains. “It’s very different from a setting like chess, where the best move is still the best move no matter how often you’ve played it.” Stratego is often used to model imperfect information situations. In this board wargame, which resembles military chess, players arrange 40 pieces on their side of a board and then move pieces across the board to capture their opponent’s flag.  But the identity of all pieces remains secret until they collide, and then the lower-ranking piece is eliminated. The possible piece configurations number more than 10 to the 66th power — an exponentially greater number than in chess — making Stratego extremely difficult for an AI system to play well.  Past efforts, such as Google’s DeepMind, relied on sophisticated operations that were computationally demanding and costly. But even with millions of dollars in training costs, these models were still not strong enough to beat top human Stratego players. “With Stratego, there is an explosion of possible universes you might have to deal with. AI techniques that were developed for games like poker definitely could not scale in this setting,” Farina says. The MIT researchers set out to develop a full AI system that could achieve superhuman performance for less cost, which they called Ataraxos (a Greek word used to describe one who is unbothered or free from anxiety). A two-pronged approach To build Ataraxos, the researchers trained the model using a technique called self-play reinforcement learning. The model plays against itself many times to learn a strong “blueprint strategy” of how to excel at Stratego.  They designed especially efficient algorithms, which enabled Ataraxos to learn much faster than prior methods while ensuring it didn’t get stuck trying to predict every possible move. This reduces training costs and boosts performance.  “Our system reaches strictly higher playing strength than DeepNash (DeepMind’s system) while using less than one hundredth of the training examples and less than one thirtieth of the self-play games, indicating a massive improvement in efficiency,” says Farina. During a game, Ataraxos uses the blueprint strategy as a starting point to set up the board and begin thinking about its next moves at each round of play.  But before acting, it refines its choices on the fly using a technique called decision-time planning. The system employs a generative model that uses probabilities to estimate the likely identities of the opponent’s hidden pieces, then evaluates future choices before selecting the next move.  “Rather than just guessing blindly, we use decision-time planning to find the most plausible state of the board. Using this generative model allows us to really zoom in on the specific board and opponent we are facing,” Farina says. The innovative use of this generative model for decision-time planning was the missing piece that enabled Ataraxos to achieve superhuman performance. Ataraxos beat the strongest Stratego player in the world by a record margin of 15-1-4 and achieved a 39-2 record against top human players at the Stratego world championship. “Ataraxos is good at calculating risk in a way that humans are not. A human might start freaking out if their most valuable piece is exposed, but the bot can be surprisingly composed. It doesn’t overcorrect and give away its secrets,” Farina says. The researchers also adapted Ataraxos for other imperfect information games, including Barrage Stratego (a faster-paced variant with fewer pieces), Hanabi (a cooperative card game with many players), and Dou dizhu (a game in which two players cooperate against a third). The system achieved superhuman performance in each instance, demonstrating the generality of this method. In the future, the researchers want to build interpretability measures into Ataraxos so the system can explain its decision-making in a way that a human could understand.  “Humans must have the final say in whether a recommendation is followed, so before adoption can happen, we need a way to audit the model’s decisions. We still have a long way to go, but I hope these algorithms can be the foundation for a lot more work to come,” Farina says. This research is funded, in part, by the Office of Naval Research, the New York University Department of Civil and Urban Engineering, the C2SMART Center, the National Science Foundation, and a Schmidt Sciences AI2050 Early Career Fellowship.
ec16b4358543dd99: ROMPIN: An Afghan tourist drowned during a diving activity near Kampung Salang, off Pulau Tioman.
